newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk army helicopter crashes in Iraq, killing 11.
newsitem.headline: Turk army helicopter crashes in Iraq, killing 11.

text.p: A Turkish helicopter on a cross-border mission against Kurdish rebels in northern Iraq crashed on Wednesday, killing 11 military personnel including two high-ranking officers, security officials said.
Officials from the emergency rule governor's office in the southeast Turkish city of Diyarbakir said the Cougar troop carrier went down in Iraq's mountainous Zap region.
The semi-official Anatolian news agency said the helicopter had suffered a technical failure but state-run television said it was not clear what had caused the crash.
A spokesman for the pro-Kurdish television channel Med TV said Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas brought down a helicopter early on Wednesday during fighting in the Zap region.
"The helicopter was shot down with a Sam-7 rocket at around seven o'clock (0400 GMT)," the spokesman said.

The helicopter was hit as it was ferrying officers off Sikifta-Birindera mountain as a PKK attack drew close to over-running the peak, the spokesman said. Clashes were continuing with the remaining soldiers, he said.
Turkish officials confirmed that eEight of the crash victims were officers, two of them high ranking.
At least 10,000 Turkish troops, backed by air power, have been in northern Iraq since May 14 in pursuit of PKK rebels who use the region as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.

Med TV said on Tuesday there was heavy fighting in northern Iraq with the PKK launching counter-attacks against the Turkish army and their Iraqi Kurdish allies and retaking a strategic mountain peak from the army.

Iraqi opposition sources say the rebels have shot down two Turkish helicopters earlier in the operation. "It seems they (the PKK) have anti-aircraft missiles and they know how to use them," an Iraqi source said.
Ankara has previously acknowleged the loss of one chopper because of what it says was a technical fault. The sky was clear over neighbouring southeast Turkey on Wednesday morning, witnesses said.
The operation has been conducted under a news blackout, making independent confirmation of reports impossible.

The incursion has attracted condemnation from the Arab League secretariat and a demand that Turkish forces withdraw immediately. Some of NATO-member Turkey's Western allies and the United Nations secretary general have criticised the operation.
Iraq's Kurds, protected from Baghdad by Western air power, took hold of the north of the country after the 1991 Gulf War.
Turkey says its forces have killed more than 2,000 rebels in the operation so far, but it has not given regular figures for government losses.
Anatolian reported the funeral on Wednesday of a soldier killed in northern Iraq after stepping on a mine. Four soldiers killed in Iraq were buried on Tuesday.
The rebels say they have killed 791 men from the opposite side -- Turkish soldiers, their allies in a "village guard" militia and guerrillas of Iraq's Kurdistan Democratic Party.
A leading PKK member this week threatened worldwide attacks against Israeli and U.S. targets if the two countries continued to "support Turkish massacres against Kurds".
